items.title: python-cq
items.text:
python-cq is an async-first Python library for organizing code around CQRS. It routes commands, queries, and events to their handlers through dedicated buses, and lets you put a queue in front of any of them when a message should be processed later. Dependency injection is pluggable behind a small protocol.

The library is made of two independent parts:

  • Routing: messages, handlers, buses, middlewares, and command pipelines. This is the core of the library and what most applications need.
  • Queuing: a Queue protocol and a Pump that drains a queue into any async callable, typically a bus.

You can use routing without ever touching queuing, and the queuing primitives work with any dispatcher, not only the buses of this library.

items.title: What is CQRS?
items.text:
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits read operations from write operations. Each operation has a single, well-defined responsibility, which:

  • clarifies intent: a CreateUserCommand does one thing, and its name says so;
  • keeps handlers small: one message, one handler, easy to test in isolation;
  • makes side effects explicit: events fan out to subscribers without coupling the producer to them.

CQRS is often discussed alongside distributed systems and Event Sourcing, but the pattern is just as useful in a local or monolithic application. The boundaries it draws are valuable on their own.

items.title: Three message types
items.text:
Type Intent Handlers Returns Command Change the state of the system Exactly one The handler's return value Query Read state without side effects Exactly one The handler's return value Event Notify that something has happened Zero, one, or many Nothing

A Command is allowed to return a value (for convenience, typically an id or a result object), but that does not make it a query. Keep intent clear.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Requires Python 3.12 or higher.

With the default DI backend (python-injection, recommended):

pip install "python-cq[injection]"

Without dependency injection (you will need to implement a DIAdapter to inject anything into your handlers):

pip install python-cq

items.title: Quickstart
items.text:
import asyncio
from cq import CommandBus, command_handler
from dataclasses import dataclass
from injection import inject


@dataclass
class CreateUserCommand:
    name: str
    email: str


@command_handler
class CreateUserHandler:
    async def handle(self, command: CreateUserCommand) -> int:
        # ... persist the user, return its id
        return 42


@inject
async def main(bus: CommandBus[int]) -> None:
    command = CreateUserCommand(name="Ada", email="ada@example.com")
    user_id = await bus.dispatch(command)
    print(f"Created user {user_id}")


asyncio.run(main())

The decorator registers the handler against the type annotation of the first handle parameter. The bus is resolved by the DI container and forwards the command to that handler.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Familiarity with the following helps you get the most out of python-cq:

  • CQRS, in particular the distinction between Commands, Queries, and Events.
  • Domain Driven Design (DDD), particularly aggregates and bounded contexts, which complement CQRS well.

items.title: python-injection
items.text:
python-injection is the default DI backend of python-cq. Install it with the [injection] extra:

pip install "python-cq[injection]"

With the extra installed, the default router uses cq.ext.injection.InjectionAdapter, so there is nothing to wire. This page describes what the adapter sets up, and how to tune it.

items.title: What is wired
items.text:
• Handlers are built through the container on every dispatch: each constructor parameter is resolved from its type annotation.
  • Buses: CommandBus, EventBus, and QueryBus are registered as fallbacks, so they can be injected right away, and any factory you register for them takes precedence (see Configuring a bus).
  • Command scope: each command dispatch opens a python-injection scope named CQScope.COMMAND_DISPATCH. RelatedEvents is registered in this scope, which is what makes it injectable in command handlers.
  • Pipelines resolve the buses from the container each time they dispatch a message.

Everything is registered in the default python-injection module, the one used by the @injectable, @inject, and @scoped decorators imported from injection.

items.title: Dependencies scoped to a command
items.text:
The command scope is a regular python-injection scope, so your own dependencies can live in it too. A dependency declared with @scoped(CQScope.COMMAND_DISPATCH) is created once per command dispatch, and shared by everything resolved during that dispatch. A typical use is a transaction shared by several repositories:

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from cq.ext.injection import CQScope
from injection import scoped


@scoped(CQScope.COMMAND_DISPATCH)
async def transaction_factory(database: Database) -> AsyncIterator[Transaction]:
    async with database.transaction() as transaction:
        yield transaction

Every repository that depends on Transaction receives the same one during a command dispatch, so everything the command writes is committed together when its dispatch ends, or rolled back if it raises. The next command gets a new transaction. Database and Transaction stand for whatever your storage library provides.

Resolving a dependency of the command scope outside a command dispatch raises a python-injection ScopeUndefinedError.

Warning

The command scope belongs to the command handler only. An event handler must not depend on anything scoped to CQScope.COMMAND_DISPATCH, even for an event published through RelatedEvents. Where and when related events are handled is a configuration choice: they may be sent to a queue and handled after the command, or in another process. Even when they are dispatched in-process, they can run while the scope is closing, and resolving the dependency then raises a python-injection ScopeError. Put what an event handler needs in the event itself, or give it its own dependencies.

items.title: Sending related events to a queue
items.text:
By default, related events are dispatched on the EventBus before the command dispatch returns. To handle them later instead, register your own RelatedEvents in the command scope. It takes precedence over the default one:

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from cq import AnyIORelatedEvents, RelatedEvents
from cq.ext.injection import CQScope
from injection import scoped


@scoped(CQScope.COMMAND_DISPATCH)
async def related_events_factory(
    queue: EventQueue,
) -> AsyncIterator[RelatedEvents]:
    async with AnyIORelatedEvents(queue) as events:
        yield events

AnyIORelatedEvents takes the function that emits each event. A queue's producer is callable, so it fits here. The command dispatch now only waits for the events to be sent, and a Pump drains the queue into the EventBus. EventQueue stands for the queue registered in your container, for example a MemoryQueue subclass or your own transport.

items.title: Custom module
items.text:
To register everything in another python-injection module than the default one, build a Router with your own InjectionAdapter, as described in Custom DI adapter:

from cq import Router
from cq.ext.injection import InjectionAdapter
from enum import StrEnum
from injection import mod


class Profile(StrEnum):
    APP = "app"


router = Router(InjectionAdapter(mod(Profile.APP))).register_defaults()

InjectionAdapter accepts two parameters:

  • module: the python-injection module where handlers are resolved and buses are registered. Defaults to the default module.
  • threadsafe: forwarded to python-injection whenever the adapter resolves a dependency or opens the command scope. With True, the resolution is wrapped in a lock. Defaults to None, which leaves the choice to python-injection.

items.title: Opening a scope around other dispatches
items.text:
cq.ext.injection.InjectionScopeMiddleware is the middleware behind the command scope. Add it to any bus, pipeline, or pump to open a python-injection scope around each message:

from cq import Pump
from cq.ext.injection import InjectionScopeMiddleware
from enum import StrEnum


class DIScope(StrEnum):
    MESSAGE = "message"


pump = Pump(queue, event_bus).add_middlewares(InjectionScopeMiddleware(DIScope.MESSAGE))

Opening a scope that is already open raises a python-injection ScopeAlreadyDefinedError. Pass exist_ok=True to reuse the open scope instead, for example when the same middleware can be nested in another dispatch:

InjectionScopeMiddleware(DIScope.MESSAGE, exist_ok=True)

It also accepts threadsafe, with the same meaning as on InjectionAdapter.

items.title: Pump
items.text:
Pump connects a Consumer to a dispatcher. The dispatcher is any async callable that accepts one message: a bus, a function, or another queue's producer.

from cq import EventBus, MemoryQueue, Pump

event_bus: EventBus = ...
queue: MemoryQueue[UserCreatedEvent] = MemoryQueue()

async with Pump(queue, event_bus).draining():
    # ...
    await queue.send(UserCreatedEvent(user_id=42))

While the draining context is open, a background task consumes the queue and passes each message to the dispatcher. On exit, the task is cancelled by default, which stops the pump right away even if some messages are still in flight.

Pump has no error policy of its own. Failures of the processing are the dispatcher's business (retries, dead letters, logging), and failures of the transport are the queue's.

items.title: Graceful shutdown
items.text:
Pass graceful=True to let the pump finish what is already queued before the context exits. The pump stops once the consumer's iteration ends, so the queue must be closed, otherwise the context waits forever for the next message:

async with Pump(queue, event_bus).draining(graceful=True):
    # ...
    await queue.send(event_1)
    await queue.send(event_2)
    # ...
    await queue.close()

items.title: Draining without a context
items.text:
draining suits a pump that runs alongside other code. When consuming the queue is all a process does, as in a dedicated worker, await drain directly:

await Pump(queue, event_bus).drain()

drain returns once the consumer's iteration ends, that is when the queue is closed, and runs forever otherwise. fail_silently and the pump's middlewares apply as with draining. Since there is no task group, an exception comes out of drain as is, not inside an ExceptionGroup.

drain runs a single drain loop. For concurrency, start several of them in your own task group, against a consumer that supports concurrent iteration (see Concurrency).

items.title: MemoryQueue.draining
items.text:
For a MemoryQueue, draining combines both steps: it opens a graceful pump, yields the queue, and closes it on exit, so the queue cannot be reused afterwards. When the block ends, every message sent inside it has been processed:

from cq import MemoryQueue

async with MemoryQueue().draining(event_bus) as queue:
    # ...
    await queue.send(event_1)
    await queue.send(event_2)

# Both events have been dispatched here.

concurrency, fail_silently, and middlewares are forwarded to the underlying Pump.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
By default, an exception raised while processing a message stops the pump, cancels the code running inside the draining block, and propagates out of draining, inside an ExceptionGroup since the pump runs in a task group. Set fail_silently=True to swallow individual failures and keep consuming the rest of the queue:

Pump(queue, event_bus, fail_silently=True)

Use it when each message is independent and one failed dispatch must not take the whole consumer down. Reporting the failures is the dispatcher's job, typically through a middleware on the bus.

The delivery sees the exception either way, so a queue can still reject the message before the pump moves on.

items.title: Concurrency
items.text:
A single drain loop pulls and dispatches messages one at a time, so the pump paces itself on the dispatcher's speed. Pass concurrency=N to draining to run N drain loops against the same consumer:

async with Pump(queue, event_bus).draining(concurrency=4):
    # ...

The consumer must support concurrent iteration. MemoryQueue does, since it wraps an anyio memory stream; if you write your own, make sure its __aiter__ can be consumed from several tasks at once.

Ordering is no longer guaranteed with concurrency > 1: a fast dispatch overtakes a slow one even if the queue delivers messages in order.

items.title: Middlewares
items.text:
A Pump has its own middleware stack, added with add_middlewares. A middleware wraps the processing of each message. It is either an async generator that yields where the dispatcher runs, or a function that takes call_next first and calls it:

async def sentry_middleware(message):
    try:
        yield
    except Exception as exc:
        sentry_sdk.capture_exception(exc)
        raise


async def timing_middleware(call_next, message):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = await call_next(message)
    print(f"Processed in {time.perf_counter() - start}s")
    return result


pump = Pump(queue, event_bus).add_middlewares(sentry_middleware, timing_middleware)

These are the same middlewares as on a bus, so everything described in the routing middlewares guide applies, including the built-in ones and the execution order. The exception is resolve_handler_source, which needs a handler behind call_next and therefore only works on a bus.

When the dispatcher is a bus, both stacks apply. Put each concern where it belongs:

  • On the pump: what is tied to the consumption cycle, such as reporting failures that escape the dispatcher.
  • On the bus: what is tied to handling the message, such as validation, business retries, or transactional boundaries.

fail_silently=True also swallows exceptions raised by a pump middleware, so a middleware that means to stop the pump is suppressed in that mode.

items.title: Queues
items.text:
Some workloads benefit from a queue between the code that produces a message and the code that processes it: smoothing bursts, keeping slow work out of the request path, or detaching the processing from the lifecycle of the caller. python-cq ships two building blocks for that:

  • a Queue protocol, with MemoryQueue as the in-process implementation;
  • a Pump that drains a queue into any async callable.

Neither depends on the routing part of the library. A message can be any object, and the dispatcher on the other end can be a bus, a plain function, or anything else that accepts one message.

items.title: The Queue protocol
items.text:
Queue[T] combines two protocols, kept separate so the producer side and the consumer side can be typed independently:

  • Producer[T] exposes async send(message). It is also callable, so await producer(message) is the same as await producer.send(message).
  • Consumer[T] is async iterable and yields a Delivery[T] for each incoming message.

A Delivery[T] is an async context manager around a single message. Entering it gives the message, and leaving it tells the queue that processing is over, with or without an exception. This is where a transport-specific queue plugs its acknowledgement or requeue logic. Pump handles the delivery lifecycle, so application code rarely touches Delivery directly.

Any object that satisfies these protocols can be used as a queue.

Note

If you'd like a Queue implementation for a specific library, feel free to open a discussion on GitHub.

items.title: MemoryQueue
items.text:
MemoryQueue is a thin wrapper around anyio.create_memory_object_stream. maxsize is how many messages the queue buffers before send waits for a free slot:

from cq import MemoryQueue

queue: MemoryQueue[UserCreatedEvent] = MemoryQueue(maxsize=100)
await queue.send(UserCreatedEvent(user_id=42))

The default, maxsize=0, means no buffer at all: send waits until a consumer takes the message. It keeps the producer from running ahead of the consumer, but await queue.send(...) blocks forever if nothing is draining the queue. Send from inside a draining context (see Pump), or pass maxsize=math.inf for an unbounded buffer.

close() stops the queue for good: consumers finish the messages already buffered, then their iteration ends, and a closed queue cannot be reopened. MemoryQueue is also an async context manager that closes itself on exit.

MemoryQueue fits when producer and consumer live in the same process. It is not thread-safe: send and the consumption must run on the event loop that created the queue. For cross-process or persistent queues, implement Queue against your transport.

items.title: Writing your own queue
items.text:
A custom queue implements send and __aiter__. Subclassing Queue gives you the callable behavior of Producer for free. The delivery is the place for acknowledgement: acknowledge when the processing succeeds, reject when it raises.

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from cq import Delivery, Queue


class BrokerQueue[T](Queue[T]):
    def __init__(self, client: BrokerClient, topic: str) -> None:
        self.client = client
        self.topic = topic

    async def __aiter__(self) -> AsyncIterator[Delivery[T]]:
        async for record in self.client.subscribe(self.topic):
            yield self.__deliver(record)

    async def send(self, message: T, /) -> None:
        await self.client.publish(self.topic, encode(message))

    @asynccontextmanager
    async def __deliver(self, record: Record) -> AsyncIterator[T]:
        try:
            yield decode(record.payload)
        except Exception:
            await record.reject()
            raise
        else:
            await record.ack()

BrokerClient, Record, encode, and decode stand for whatever your transport library provides. The message itself stays plain data: transport concerns live in the queue, not on the message.

The resilience of the transport (reconnecting, retrying a failed fetch) also belongs to the queue. If the iteration raises, the pump draining it stops, even with fail_silently=True, which only covers the processing of each message.

items.title: Configuring a bus
items.text:
Note

This guide assumes the [injection] extra is installed. If you use a different DI framework, register the factories below with your own container instead of @injectable.

The buses resolved by default have no listeners and no middlewares of your own. To customize one, write a factory that builds the bus with new_command_bus(), new_query_bus(), or new_event_bus(), configures it, and registers it in the DI container:

from cq import CommandBus, new_command_bus
from injection import injectable


@injectable
def command_bus_factory() -> CommandBus:
    bus = new_command_bus()
    bus.add_listeners(log_listener)
    bus.add_middlewares(timing_middleware)
    return bus

Your factory takes precedence over the default registration, so every handler, middleware, or function that depends on CommandBus now receives the configured bus. The same pattern applies to QueryBus and EventBus.

Annotate the factory with the bare CommandBus, as the default registration does. A parameterized annotation such as CommandBus[Any] registers a different type, and the default bus keeps being injected.

new_command_bus() returns a bus that already wraps each dispatch in the command scope of the DI adapter. Always start from it rather than building a bus by hand, or RelatedEvents will not be available to your command handlers.

Both add_listeners and add_middlewares accept any number of arguments and return the bus, so calls can be chained.

items.title: Listeners
items.text:
A listener is an async callable that receives the message. Its return value is ignored. Listeners suit logging, metrics, or any side effect that does not need to influence the handler:

async def log_listener(message):
    print(f"Received: {message}")

Listeners are scheduled in an anyio task group, so several listeners run concurrently. The timing depends on the bus type:

  • CommandBus and QueryBus: every listener must finish before the handler runs. dispatch then returns the handler's value as soon as it completes.
  • EventBus: listeners and handlers share the same task group, so they all run concurrently. dispatch returns once everything has finished.

A listener is not isolated from the dispatch. An exception raised by a listener escapes dispatch inside an ExceptionGroup, and on a CommandBus or a QueryBus this happens before the handler is called, so the message is never handled. Guard fragile listener code with its own try/except if it must not affect the dispatch.

A listener can also be a class with an async __call__ method, which is convenient when it needs its own dependencies:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class LogListener:
    logger: Logger

    async def __call__(self, message):
        self.logger.info(f"Received: {message}")

items.title: Middlewares
items.text: Middlewares wrap the execution of the handler, to run logic before and after it or to deal with its exceptions. They have their own page: Middlewares.

items.title: Custom DI adapter
items.text:
Note

If you installed python-cq[injection], you can skip this page. The integration with python-injection is already wired up (see python-injection). This page is only useful to plug in a different DI framework.

python-cq does not depend on a specific dependency injection container. It talks to DI through the DIAdapter protocol: implement it once and the library works with the container you already use.

items.title: The Router class
items.text:
Router ties the handler registries to a DI adapter. The decorators (command_handler, event_handler, query_handler) and bus factories (new_command_bus, new_event_bus, new_query_bus) exported by cq are bound to a default Router built at import time, which uses python-injection when the extra is installed.

To use your own adapter, create a Router with it and use its methods in place of the module-level ones:

from cq import Router

router = Router(MyDIAdapter()).register_defaults()

command_handler = router.command_handler
event_handler = router.event_handler
query_handler = router.query_handler

new_command_bus = router.new_command_bus
new_event_bus = router.new_event_bus
new_query_bus = router.new_query_bus

register_defaults() hands the bus factories to the adapter so that CommandBus, EventBus, and QueryBus can be resolved from the container. Call it once per router.

A router also lists the message types its handlers are registered for, through command_types, event_types, and query_types.

Pipelines follow the same rule. Build them from your router so they resolve the buses through your adapter:

class PaymentContext:
    pipeline: ClassVar[ContextCommandPipeline[ValidateCartCommand]] = (
        router.command_pipeline()
    )

items.title: Implementing a DIAdapter
items.text:
DIAdapter is a Protocol with four methods. lazy and wire are required, command_scope and register_defaults are optional:

from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from cq import Command, CommandBus, DIAdapter, EventBus, Middleware, QueryBus, Router
from typing import Any, Concatenate


class MyDIAdapter(DIAdapter):
    def command_scope(self) -> Middleware[Concatenate[Command, ...], Any] | None:
        """
        Return a middleware that wraps each command dispatch.

        It must create a `RelatedEvents` instance, make it resolvable for as
        long as the dispatch lasts so that command handlers can inject it,
        and wait for the scheduled events before the dispatch returns.

        Optional: by default no middleware wraps the dispatch, and command
        handlers have no `RelatedEvents` to inject.
        """
        ...

    def lazy[T](self, tp: type[T]) -> Callable[[], Awaitable[T]]:
        """
        Return a callable that, when called and awaited, resolves `tp` from
        the container. Pipelines call the returned callable on every
        message they dispatch, so that buses registered later in the import
        graph are picked up.
        """
        ...

    def register_defaults(
        self,
        command_bus: Callable[..., CommandBus[Any]],
        event_bus: Callable[..., EventBus],
        query_bus: Callable[..., QueryBus[Any]],
    ) -> None:
        """
        Register the bus factories with the container so that `CommandBus`,
        `EventBus`, and `QueryBus` can be declared as dependencies.

        Optional: the default implementation does nothing.
        """
        ...

    def wire[T](self, tp: type[T]) -> Callable[..., Awaitable[T]]:
        """
        Return an async factory that instantiates `tp` with its dependencies
        injected. Called once per handler at registration, and the factory
        is awaited on every dispatch.
        """
        ...


router = Router(MyDIAdapter()).register_defaults()

items.title: The command scope
items.text:
AnyIORelatedEvents is the ready-made RelatedEvents implementation. It is an async context manager that takes the function used to emit each event, usually an EventBus, and waits for every scheduled event on exit. A command scope typically opens one per dispatch and exposes it to the container:

from cq import AnyIORelatedEvents, EventBus, MiddlewareResult, RelatedEvents
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any


@dataclass
class CommandScopeMiddleware:
    event_bus: EventBus

    async def __call__(self, command) -> MiddlewareResult[Any]:
        async with AnyIORelatedEvents(self.event_bus) as events:
            with container.override(RelatedEvents, events):
                yield

Your adapter's command_scope returns an instance of this class, built with the event bus. container.override stands for whatever your container provides. If your container already exposes the scope as an async context manager, wrap it with cq.middlewares.contextlib.AsyncContextManagerMiddleware instead of writing the middleware by hand.

You can also write your own RelatedEvents (an outbox, an implementation that enriches events with a correlation id, ...). The protocol only requires an add(*events) method.

items.title: Passing RelatedEvents as an argument
items.text:
If your container cannot scope a dependency to a dispatch, there is a workaround: the command scope can pass RelatedEvents to the handler as an extra argument of call_next, which is forwarded down to handle. Prefer a scoped dependency whenever your container supports one.

Warning

This changes the signature of every command handler, not only those that publish events: each handle must accept the extra parameter, otherwise its dispatch raises a TypeError.

from cq import AnyIORelatedEvents, EventBus
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class CommandScopeMiddleware:
    event_bus: EventBus

    async def __call__(self, call_next, command):
        async with AnyIORelatedEvents(self.event_bus) as events:
            return await call_next(command, events)

Command handlers then receive the events as the second parameter of handle, instead of as a constructor dependency:

from cq import RelatedEvents, command_handler
from typing import NamedTuple


@command_handler
class CreateUserHandler(NamedTuple):
    repository: UserRepository

    async def handle(self, command: CreateUserCommand, events: RelatedEvents) -> int:
        user = await self.repository.create(command.name, command.email)
        events.add(UserCreatedEvent(user_id=user.id))
        return user.id

The middlewares you add to the bus are not affected: they sit outside the command scope (see Execution order) and only receive the command.

items.title: Without an adapter
items.text:
Router() without argument uses a minimal adapter: handlers are instantiated with no arguments, there is no command scope, and anything that needs to resolve a bus lazily (such as a pipeline) raises a RuntimeError as soon as it is created. This is also what the default router uses when the [injection] extra is not installed.

The reference implementation for python-injection lives in cq.ext.injection.InjectionAdapter. It is a good starting point to model your own adapter on a working example.

items.title: Dispatching messages
items.text:
python-cq exposes three bus types: CommandBus, QueryBus, and EventBus. CommandBus and QueryBus take a type parameter for the value returned by dispatch. EventBus takes none, since it returns nothing.

A bus is obtained from your DI container. With the [injection] extra, the three types are registered by default, so you can declare them as dependencies right away:

from cq import CommandBus
from injection import inject


@inject
async def create_user(bus: CommandBus[int]) -> int:
    return await bus.dispatch(CreateUserCommand(name="Ada", email="ada@example.com"))

To customize a bus with listeners or middlewares, see Configuring a bus.

items.title: CommandBus
items.text:
The CommandBus sends a command to its single handler and returns the handler's value:

from cq import CommandBus

bus: CommandBus[int] = ...
user_id = await bus.dispatch(CreateUserCommand(name="Ada", email="ada@example.com"))

Each dispatch runs inside a command scope opened by the DI adapter. This is what makes RelatedEvents injectable in command handlers.

AnyCommandBus is a shorthand for CommandBus[Any], handy when one bus dispatches commands with different return types.

items.title: QueryBus
items.text:
The QueryBus sends a query to its single handler and returns the handler's value:

from cq import QueryBus

bus: QueryBus[User] = ...
user = await bus.dispatch(GetUserByIdQuery(user_id=42))

items.title: EventBus
items.text:
The EventBus fans an event out to every registered handler. It does not return a value, since several handlers may produce conflicting results.

from cq import EventBus

bus: EventBus = ...
await bus.dispatch(UserCreatedEvent(user_id=42))

Event handlers run concurrently inside a single anyio task group. dispatch returns once every handler has finished. If a handler raises (and is not declared with fail_silently=True), the remaining handlers are cancelled and the exception comes out of dispatch inside an ExceptionGroup.

items.title: Buses are callables
items.text: Every bus is also an async callable: await bus(message) is the same as await bus.dispatch(message). This lets you pass a bus anywhere an async (message) -> result function is expected, for example as the dispatcher of a Pump.

items.title: When no handler is registered
items.text:
If no handler matches the message type, dispatch returns the NotImplemented sentinel instead of raising. This is convenient when a message is optional in some contexts (a query that may or may not have a backing handler depending on configuration), but it means a dispatch result is not always meaningful:

result = await bus.dispatch(SomeQuery())

if result is NotImplemented:
    # No handler is registered for SomeQuery.
    ...

The same sentinel is returned when a handler declared with fail_silently=True raises. For events, there is nothing to return, so the sentinel is not exposed.

items.title: Messages and handlers
items.text: This guide covers how to define messages and how to register the handlers that process them, for the three message types: Command, Query, and Event.

items.title: Messages
items.text:
A message is any Python object. Messages are pure data, so dataclass is a natural choice, but a pydantic.BaseModel, a msgspec.Struct, or any other class works just as well:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class CreateUserCommand:
    name: str
    email: str

There is no base class to inherit from. Command, Query, and Event exported by cq are aliases of object, used only to make type hints read better. A handler is matched to a message by the type annotation of its handle method, not by a marker class.

items.title: Handlers
items.text:
A handler is a class with an async handle method that takes the message as its first parameter. It is registered with one of the three decorators: @command_handler, @query_handler, or @event_handler.

from cq import command_handler


@command_handler
class CreateUserHandler:
    async def handle(self, command: CreateUserCommand) -> int: ...

The decorator reads the annotation of the first parameter of handle to know which message type the handler subscribes to. A missing annotation raises a TypeError at import time.

A new handler instance is built for every dispatch, through the configured DI adapter, so constructor dependencies are injected each time the handler runs.

A command or a query accepts a single handler: registering a second one for the same message type raises a RuntimeError as soon as the module is imported. An event accepts any number of handlers.

items.title: Declaring dependencies
items.text:
Defining a handler as a NamedTuple (or a frozen dataclass) gives a concise, immutable declaration of its dependencies:

from cq import command_handler
from typing import NamedTuple


@command_handler
class CreateUserHandler(NamedTuple):
    repository: UserRepository

    async def handle(self, command: CreateUserCommand) -> int:
        user = await self.repository.create(command.name, command.email)
        return user.id

UserRepository is resolved by the DI container when the handler is instantiated.

items.title: Explicit message type
items.text:
The message type can be passed to the decorator instead of being read from the annotation. It takes precedence over the annotation:

@command_handler(CreateUserCommand)
class CreateUserHandler:
    async def handle(self, command) -> int: ...

items.title: Polymorphic dispatch
items.text:
A handler registered for a base class also receives every subclass of that type. This lets you write a single handler for a family of related messages:

from cq import event_handler
from dataclasses import dataclass


class DomainEvent: ...


@dataclass
class UserCreatedEvent(DomainEvent):
    user_id: int


@event_handler
class AuditLogger:
    async def handle(self, event: DomainEvent):
        # Receives UserCreatedEvent and any other DomainEvent subclass.
        ...

Resolution walks the message's MRO and also understands generic aliases and type aliases. A union annotation registers the handler once per member, so event: UserCreatedEvent | UserDeletedEvent subscribes to both types.

When several handlers match through the MRO, a command or a query goes to the most specific one: a handler registered for a subclass wins over one registered for its base class. An event goes to all of them.

items.title: Command handlers
items.text:
Command handlers change the state of the system and may return a value, typically an identifier or a small result object.

from cq import command_handler
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import NamedTuple


@dataclass
class CreateUserCommand:
    name: str
    email: str


@command_handler
class CreateUserHandler(NamedTuple):
    repository: UserRepository

    async def handle(self, command: CreateUserCommand) -> int:
        user = await self.repository.create(command.name, command.email)
        return user.id

items.title: Related events
items.text:
A command handler can inject RelatedEvents to publish events as part of the command's execution:

from cq import RelatedEvents, command_handler


@command_handler
class CreateUserHandler(NamedTuple):
    repository: UserRepository
    events: RelatedEvents

    async def handle(self, command: CreateUserCommand) -> int:
        user = await self.repository.create(command.name, command.email)
        self.events.add(UserCreatedEvent(user_id=user.id))
        return user.id

events.add(...) accepts any number of events and schedules each one on a task group that lives for the duration of the command dispatch. Events start as soon as the handler gives control back to the event loop (at its next await, or when it returns) and run concurrently with the rest of the handler. The command dispatch only returns once every scheduled event has been fully handled. Where you call add therefore says something: as the last line, nothing after it depends on the event; in the middle of the handler, the remaining work runs concurrently with the event handlers.

Scheduled events are handled even if the command handler raises afterwards: nothing is rolled back. Call add once the work the event reports has actually succeeded. For the same reason, a command retried by RetryMiddleware publishes the events of every failed attempt.

If an event handler raises, the command handler is cancelled if it is still running, and the exception propagates back to the caller of the command, wrapped in two nested ExceptionGroups: one for the events scheduled by the command, one for the handlers of that event. Catch it with except*, which matches through any level of nesting.

RelatedEvents is provided by the command scope of the DI adapter. With the [injection] extra it works out of the box; with a custom adapter, see Custom DI adapter.

items.title: Query handlers
items.text:
Query handlers read state and must not produce side effects.

from cq import query_handler
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import NamedTuple


@dataclass
class GetUserByIdQuery:
    user_id: int


@query_handler
class GetUserByIdHandler(NamedTuple):
    repository: UserRepository

    async def handle(self, query: GetUserByIdQuery) -> User:
        return await self.repository.get(query.user_id)

items.title: Event handlers
items.text:
Event handlers react to something that has already happened. An event can have zero, one, or many handlers, which makes events the right tool for loose coupling between components.

from cq import event_handler
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import NamedTuple


@dataclass
class UserCreatedEvent:
    user_id: int


@event_handler
class SendWelcomeEmailHandler(NamedTuple):
    email_service: EmailService

    async def handle(self, event: UserCreatedEvent):
        await self.email_service.send_welcome(event.user_id)


@event_handler
class TrackUserCreatedHandler(NamedTuple):
    analytics: AnalyticsService

    async def handle(self, event: UserCreatedEvent):
        await self.analytics.track("user_created", event.user_id)

Both handlers receive the same event and run concurrently when it is dispatched.

items.title: fail_silently
items.text:
By default, an exception raised inside a handler propagates to the caller of dispatch. For non-critical handlers (telemetry, audit logging, best-effort notifications) you can suppress it:

@event_handler(fail_silently=True)
class TrackUserCreatedHandler(NamedTuple):
    analytics: AnalyticsService

    async def handle(self, event: UserCreatedEvent):
        # An exception here is swallowed once the middlewares have seen it.
        ...

Middlewares still see the exception before it is suppressed, so a middleware can log it or record metrics while the rest of the system carries on.

fail_silently is accepted by the three decorators. On a command or a query handler, dispatch returns the NotImplemented sentinel instead of raising.

items.title: Middlewares
items.text:
A middleware wraps the execution of a handler. Use it to run logic before and after the handler processes the message, or to deal with its exceptions. Middlewares are added to a bus with add_middlewares:

bus = new_command_bus()
bus.add_middlewares(timing_middleware, transaction_middleware)

For commands and queries, the middleware stack wraps the single handler once. For events, the stack is applied around each handler independently, so a middleware sees one invocation per event handler.

The same middlewares can be attached to a command pipeline and to a Pump.

items.title: Generator middlewares
items.text:
The simplest form is an async generator that receives the message and yields once, where the handler should run:

import time


async def timing_middleware(message):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    yield
    print(f"Execution time: {time.perf_counter() - start}s")

The yield behaves like a try/finally around the handler call. An exception raised by the handler is thrown at the yield, so you can catch it there:

async def logging_middleware(message):
    try:
        yield
    except Exception:
        logger.exception("Failed to handle %r", message)
        raise

result = yield receives the handler's return value, but only for inspection: a generator middleware cannot replace it. This keeps the message and the result read-only by default. If the middleware swallows an exception instead of re-raising it, dispatch returns the NotImplemented sentinel.

After an exception, the middleware may yield again to call the handler one more time. This is how RetryMiddleware is written. Yielding again after a successful call raises cq.exceptions.MiddlewareError.

The return annotation for these middlewares is MiddlewareResult[T], where T is the handler's return type:

from cq import MiddlewareResult
from typing import Any


async def timing_middleware(message: Any) -> MiddlewareResult[Any]:
    ...
    yield

items.title: Classic middlewares
items.text:
When you need to replace the return value, or to skip the handler and return something else instead, write a "classic" middleware. It takes call_next as its first argument and returns the value it wants to expose to the caller:

async def cache_middleware(call_next, query):
    if (cached := cache.get(query)) is not None:
        return cached

    result = await call_next(query)
    cache.set(query, result)
    return result

Both styles can be mixed freely on the same bus. Middleware is the type alias that covers both.

items.title: Finding the handler
items.text:
resolve_handler_source(call_next) returns the handler class behind call_next, so a classic middleware knows which handler is about to run, typically to log or trace it:

from cq import resolve_handler_source


async def logging_middleware(call_next, message):
    handler_type = resolve_handler_source(call_next)
    logger.info("%s handles %r", handler_type.__name__, message)
    return await call_next(message)

The class also gives access to metadata declared on the handler, such as a class attribute or a marker set by your own decorator.

It only works on a bus. On a Pump or a pipeline, there is no handler behind call_next, and it raises an AttributeError.

items.title: Class-based middlewares
items.text:
Both styles can also be written as a class with an async __call__ method, which is convenient when the middleware needs its own dependencies:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class TimingMiddleware:
    metrics: MetricsService

    async def __call__(self, message):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        yield
        await self.metrics.record(time.perf_counter() - start)


@dataclass
class CacheMiddleware:
    cache: Cache

    async def __call__(self, call_next, query): ...

If you build these classes through your DI container (for example as parameters of the bus factory), you get the same constructor injection as for handlers.

items.title: Execution order
items.text:
Middlewares nest around the handler like the layers of an onion. Within one call, they run in the order you list them: the first argument is the outermost layer, so it starts first and finishes last.

bus.add_middlewares(outer, inner)
# outer -> inner -> handler -> inner -> outer

Each subsequent call wraps whatever is already registered, so the middlewares added last end up outermost:

bus.add_middlewares(a, b)  # a -> b -> handler
bus.add_middlewares(c)  # c -> a -> b -> handler

The rule also covers the command scope that new_command_bus() installs before you add anything. Your own middlewares sit outside of it: they wrap the dispatch of every related event, but they cannot inject a dependency that only exists inside the scope, such as RelatedEvents.

items.title: RetryMiddleware
items.text:
cq.middlewares.retry.RetryMiddleware calls the handler again when it raises one of the configured exception types:

from cq.middlewares.retry import RetryMiddleware

bus.add_middlewares(RetryMiddleware(retry=3, delay=0.5, exceptions=(TimeoutError,)))
  • retry: total number of attempts, including the first one. With retry=3, the handler runs at most three times. Must be at least 1.
  • delay: seconds to wait between attempts. Defaults to 0.
  • exceptions: the exception types that trigger a retry. Defaults to (Exception,).

If every attempt fails, the last exception is re-raised.

items.title: CaptureExceptionMiddleware
items.text:
cq.middlewares.exc.CaptureExceptionMiddleware catches exceptions raised downstream and forwards them to a callback. Use it to log, report, or push errors to an external sink:

from cq.middlewares.exc import CaptureExceptionMiddleware


async def report(exception, message):
    sentry_sdk.capture_exception(exception)


bus.add_middlewares(CaptureExceptionMiddleware(report, reraise=True))
  • on_error: an async callback invoked with the captured exception followed by the arguments the handler received (the message). Use CaptureExceptionMiddleware.sync(...) if your callback is synchronous.
  • exceptions: the exception types to capture. Defaults to (Exception,).
  • reraise: whether to re-raise the exception after the callback returns. Defaults to False, in which case the exception is swallowed.

on_error is meant for side effects only and must not raise. If it does, its own exception propagates in place of the original one.

items.title: Context manager middlewares
items.text:
cq.middlewares.contextlib turns an existing context manager into a middleware that wraps every dispatch:

  • ContextManagerMiddleware(context) for a synchronous context manager;
  • AsyncContextManagerMiddleware(context) for an asynchronous one.
from contextlib import suppress
from cq.middlewares.contextlib import ContextManagerMiddleware

bus.add_middlewares(ContextManagerMiddleware(suppress(LookupError)))

The same context manager instance is entered on every dispatch, so it must be reusable. Context managers built with @contextmanager are single-use and do not fit here.

items.title: Executing multiple commands
items.text:
In CQRS, the saga pattern is the usual way to orchestrate a sequence of commands. Sagas are designed for distributed systems and can feel overengineered for a local workflow. python-cq offers two lightweight alternatives for running several commands in-process:

  • dispatch_sequentially when the messages are known up front and do not depend on each other's results;
  • ContextCommandPipeline when each command is built from the result of the previous one.

items.title: dispatch_sequentially
items.text:
dispatch_sequentially takes a dispatcher and any number of messages. It dispatches them in the given order, waiting for each one to complete before starting the next, and returns the results as a tuple in the same order.

A typical use is to drive the system into a known state through its own commands, for example when setting up a test:

from cq import AnyCommandBus, dispatch_sequentially

bus: AnyCommandBus = ...
account_id = 42

_, _, subscription = await dispatch_sequentially(
    bus,
    CreateAccountCommand(account_id=account_id, email="ada@example.com"),
    SubscribeToPlanCommand(account_id=account_id, plan="pro"),
    SuspendSubscriptionCommand(account_id=account_id, reason="payment_failed"),
)

Each command goes through the real handlers and middlewares, so the resulting state is exactly what the application would produce. The dispatcher can be any Dispatcher: a CommandBus, a QueryBus, or an EventBus. If a handler raises, the exception propagates immediately and the remaining messages are not dispatched.

The result tuple is typed with a variadic type parameter that cannot be inferred from the arguments, so annotate the target to get precise element types:

results: tuple[Account, Subscription, Subscription] = await dispatch_sequentially(
    bus,
    create_account,
    subscribe,
    suspend,
)

Each message is dispatched exactly as bus.dispatch would, so the NotImplemented sentinel can appear in the tuple when a message has no handler.

items.title: ContextCommandPipeline
items.text:
A pipeline runs a sequence of commands. Each step receives the result of the previous command and produces the next command to dispatch. The class that holds the pipeline is the context: instance attributes assigned in one step are visible in the next.

from cq import ContextCommandPipeline
from typing import ClassVar


class PaymentContext:
    transaction_id: int

    pipeline: ClassVar[ContextCommandPipeline[ValidateCartCommand]] = (
        ContextCommandPipeline()
    )

    @pipeline.step
    def _(self, result: CartValidatedResult) -> CreateTransactionCommand:
        return CreateTransactionCommand(cart_id=result.cart_id, amount=result.total)

    @pipeline.step
    def _(self, result: TransactionCreatedResult) -> NotifyMerchantCommand:
        self.transaction_id = result.transaction_id
        return NotifyMerchantCommand(transaction_id=result.transaction_id)

    @pipeline.step
    def _(self, result: MerchantNotifiedResult): ...

Annotate the pipeline with ClassVar: if the context is a dataclass, a plain annotation would turn the pipeline into a field.

The pipeline resolves CommandBus and QueryBus from the DI container each time it dispatches a message, not when it is created, so the buses you configure in your container are the ones it uses. With a bus factory registered as @injectable, each message is therefore dispatched by a new bus. If you manage your own Router (see Custom DI adapter), build the pipeline with router.command_pipeline() instead.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
A step is a method decorated with @pipeline.step. It receives the value returned by the previous command's handler and returns the next command to dispatch. Steps can be sync or async.

A step that returns None stops the pipeline. This is the natural way to write a terminal step that only consumes the previous result, and it also lets earlier steps abort the pipeline conditionally:

@pipeline.step
def _(self, result: ValidationResult) -> PersistCommand | None:
    if not result.is_valid:
        return None  # stop here, skip the rest of the pipeline

    return PersistCommand(...)

items.title: Query steps
items.text:
@pipeline.query_step works like @pipeline.step, but the message it produces is dispatched through the QueryBus:

@pipeline.query_step
def _(self, result: TransactionCreatedResult) -> GetMerchantByIdQuery:
    return GetMerchantByIdQuery(merchant_id=result.merchant_id)

items.title: Static steps
items.text:
When a step does not depend on the previous result, declare it with add_static_step (for a command) or add_static_query_step (for a query). The given message is dispatched as is each time the pipeline runs:

class WarmCacheContext:
    pipeline: ClassVar[ContextCommandPipeline[StartCommand]] = ContextCommandPipeline()

    pipeline.add_static_step(LoadConfigCommand())
    pipeline.add_static_query_step(GetActiveUsersQuery())

    @pipeline.step
    def _(self, users: list[User]) -> WarmCacheCommand:
        return WarmCacheCommand(user_ids=[user.id for user in users])

Static and decorated steps run in the order they are declared in the class body.

items.title: Running a pipeline
items.text:
Calling Context.pipeline(initial_command) builds a fresh Context instance, runs every step against it, and returns the populated context:

async def process_payment(cart_id: int) -> int:
    context = await PaymentContext.pipeline(ValidateCartCommand(cart_id=cart_id))
    return context.transaction_id

Each run gets its own context instance, so attributes set in one run do not leak into the next. The instance is created when Context.pipeline is accessed, not when it is called: keeping run = Context.pipeline and calling it twice reuses the same instance. The context class is instantiated without arguments in this form.

items.title: Seeding the context
items.text:
If a step needs values that are known before the first command runs, instantiate the context yourself and call pipeline on the instance. The same object is returned at the end, mutated by every step that ran.

Because the input and the returned context are the same object, the recommended pattern is to hide both behind a run classmethod:

from cq import ContextCommandPipeline
from typing import ClassVar, Self
from uuid import UUID


class LinkOAuthAccountContext:
    pipeline: ClassVar[ContextCommandPipeline[VerifyIDTokenCommand]] = (
        ContextCommandPipeline()
    )

    def __init__(self, user_id: UUID, provider: OAuthProvider) -> None:
        self.user_id = user_id
        self.provider = provider

    @pipeline.step
    def _(self, user: OAuthUser) -> LinkOAuthAccountCommand:
        return LinkOAuthAccountCommand(
            user_id=self.user_id,
            provider=self.provider,
            provider_user_id=user.id,
            email=user.email,
        )

    @classmethod
    async def run(cls, user_id: UUID, command: VerifyIDTokenCommand) -> Self:
        return await cls(user_id, command.provider).pipeline(command)

The initial VerifyIDTokenCommand carries the token and the provider, but not the user. Once the OAuth identity is verified, the step that builds LinkOAuthAccountCommand uses the seeded user_id (taken from the auth context) and provider (read from the input command), so callers only pass user_id and the command to run.

items.title: Middlewares
items.text:
A pipeline accepts middlewares with add_middlewares, with the same syntax as a bus (see Middlewares):

class PaymentContext:
    pipeline: ClassVar[ContextCommandPipeline[ValidateCartCommand]] = (
        ContextCommandPipeline().add_middlewares(
            timing_middleware,
            transaction_middleware,
        )
    )

Pipeline middlewares wrap the whole run, not each step, and receive the initial command. The middlewares configured on the underlying CommandBus still apply to every command the pipeline dispatches.
